articles.title: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
articles.summary: The COP31 summit in Antalya was the longest-running climate talks in UN history.
articles.body:
The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.

The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.

Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.

After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.

Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".

The world is preparing for life beyond 1.5C

This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.

The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.

Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.

Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:

Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding

The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life

Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world

Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.

"This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.

The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible – it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).

This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.

Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.

There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial and are not well advanced.

Countries divided over approach on fossil fuels

This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.

On the central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts – countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.

And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.

Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.

This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.

If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.

Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed

Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.

"The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".

That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".

Russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".

It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other issues to tackle problems they can't solve alone.

Much of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.

But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.

On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.

In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms.

And some of those were agreed at the talks.

The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits – money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases – will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.

They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.

But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.

Renewable energy growth remains unstoppable

What governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.

The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook points to another powerful force: energy security.

It says the disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz has been the biggest energy supply shock in history. The longer the uncertainty continues, the stronger the incentive for countries to switch from imported fossil fuels to electricity generated at home.

Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles have become increasingly competitive.

As clean energy develops its own commercial momentum, formal negotiations may become less important in determining its direction and pace.

Against the headwinds of inflation new investment announcements emerged at COP as part of the "Action Agenda".

This is the part of the COP process that tries to mobilise action outside of formal talks from businesses, investors and cities – this year the focus was on electrification. Turning more of our energy from fossil fuels to electricity.

"We are not entering the age of electricity, we have arrived at the age of electricity," Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, told the BBC. He says energy security and climate policies are now "closely aligned".

Governments still have a crucial role in facilitating the transition, according to Dr Jennie Dodson, a senior director at the World Business Council for Sustainable Development which includes among its members the likes of Amazon and Apple.

"A key message from business is we can go so far, a lot of it is cost competitive, but there are policy barriers both around infrastructure and permitting".

COP31 has shown how the role of these annual UN climate conferences is changing.

For the first 30 COPs, the emphasis was on building the international framework for tackling global warming.

The great diplomatic breakthrough came in Paris in 2015, when almost every country agreed to keep global warming well below 2°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.

Paris also established machinery designed to turn promises into progress. Every five years, governments assess collective progress in a global stocktake and submit new national climate plans, known as NDCs.

Then came further agreements: a fund for climate damage at COP27, a commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and triple renewable energy capacity at COP28, a new climate finance target at COP29 and increased support for adaptation at COP30.

The international architecture for tackling climate change has, in other words, largely been built.

Now comes the harder business of making it work. That's why this year's conference in Antalya, Turkey, had been billed as an "implementation COP".

The emphasis now is shifting towards delivering commitments already made. Camilla Born, who helped develop the UK's strategy for COP26 and now heads the campaign group Electrify Britain, told the BBC this is making COP more procedural - less about fundamental negotiations than ensuring the machinery actually works.

This could mean doing away with a cover text – the central political agreement that countries sign up to with new pledges.

It is not a requirement to have one, and for many years countries managed without. Australia chose to push one for this COP, and it is where they fell down.

On many of the procedural issues Camilla Born spoke of, they did agree things. That may be important. It isn't necessarily exciting.

And there is a fundamental limit to what this machinery can achieve. Under the Paris Agreement countries have no mechanism to force them to meet their emissions targets.

So, when critics berate the COP process for failing to tackle the problem fast enough, it isn't really the system that is at fault, says Alden Meyer, a veteran climate negotiator now at the climate think tank E3G.

The COP process, he suggests, is "like a mirror that we hold up to ourselves every year". If the reflection is disappointing, the problem is the governments, not the mirror.

articles.title: DR Congo conflict: Kenya's William Ruto and Félix Tshisekedi agree to restore ties
articles.summary: The two leaders committed to upholding sovereignty and "non-interference in the internal affairs of states".
articles.body:
Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.

This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.

On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".

The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé as mediator.

Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".

DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).

DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.

DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.

When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.

The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.

DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.

Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader

Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila , in October 2025.

Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.

He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.

Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.

The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.

On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.

Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.

More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.

The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

articles.title: Ayodhya-Janakpur train, Rs 15,000 crore package, 8 MoUs: Key takeaways from PM Modi and Balen Shah meet
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India and Nepal on Monday signed eight agreements to expand cooperation in sectors including space technology, security, healthcare,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India and Nepal on Monday signed eight agreements to expand cooperation in sectors including space technology, security, healthcare, agriculture and sustainable urban development, following talks between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah in New Delhi.The two leaders also virtually flagged off the Saryu-Kamala Express, connecting Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh with Janakpur in Nepal, and jointly inaugurated several development projects during Balen Shah’s two-day state visit to India.At a joint press conference after the talks, Modi said the two countries had taken several important decisions to strengthen bilateral relations.“I am very pleased to welcome Balendra Shah ji to India on his first bilateral visit after becoming the Prime Minister of Nepal. A few months ago, when he addressed the United Nations as the world’s youngest Prime Minister, we got a clear glimpse of his vision. Over the past few hours of our discussions, I have sensed his clear vision and commitment towards Nepal’s future and India-Nepal relations. The historic mandate given to him by the people of Nepal this year reflects the aspirations and hopes of the country’s younger generation. India has always been a partner in the development journey of a strong and prosperous Nepal. In this spirit, today we have taken several important decisions to take our relations to new heights,” PM Modi said.The prime minister also announced a development cooperation package of 24,000 crore Nepali rupees (approximately Rs 15,000 crore) to support Nepal’s reconstruction and long-term development, particularly in the wake of the devastating floods in August.“We express our deep condolences for the loss of lives caused by the devastating floods in Nepal in August. Today, we announce a development cooperation package of 24,000 crore Nepali rupees to give fresh impetus to Nepal’s reconstruction and long-term development. Our commitment will be to help affected families get their lives back on track, create new opportunities, and further strengthen Nepal’s capacity to deal with future disasters,” he said.PM Modi also highlighted the shared religious and cultural ties between the two countries, referring to the launch of the train service connecting Ayodhya and Janakpur.“Lord Ram and Mata Sita are symbols of our shared civilisation and faith. In 2018, on the sacred land of Janakpur, I had said that our pilgrimage sites are incomplete without Nepal, and our Lord Ram is incomplete without Nepal. In 2024, the consecration ceremony of Ram Lalla took place in Ayodhya. This historic occasion gave renewed strength to our shared faith…With the launch of the Sarayu-Kamala Express train service today, we are giving a new dimension to this sacred bond,” he said.He said India had maintained supplies of fuel and other essential goods to Nepal despite serious challenges related to oil supplies this year, and expressed confidence in the future of bilateral ties.“We will together write a golden chapter of India-Nepal relations,” PM Modi said.Saryu-Kamala Express to connect Ayodhya and JanakpurThe Saryu-Kamala Express will connect Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh with Janakpur Dham in Nepal, covering around 604 km in approximately 19 hours. The regular service will operate once a week in each direction from November 28, enabling pilgrims to travel between the two religious destinations without changing trains.The inaugural run on Monday operated as a special train (No. 04295), departing from Ayodhya Dham at 12.30 pm.Eight agreements signed across key sectorsThe eight MoUs exchanged after the delegation-level talks cover satellite communication, policing, forensic sciences, civil service training, healthcare, traditional medicine, sustainable urban development, and livestock and fisheries development.In the space and communication sector, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and Nepal’s Ministry of Information and Communication signed an MoU to establish a Satellite Communication (SATCOM) Network for the utilisation of the South Asia Satellite.Two agreements aim to strengthen cooperation in policing and forensic sciences. One provides for academic and research collaboration between the National Forensic Sciences University in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, and the Crime Investigation Department of Nepal Police. The other was signed between India’s Rashtriya Raksha University and Nepal’s National Police Academy.For capacity building in public administration, the National Centre for Good Governance, under India’s Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances, signed an MoU with Nepal’s Administrative Staff College under the Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration. The agreement provides for training programmes for Nepalese civil servants.In healthcare, India’s Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and Nepal’s Ministry of Health and Food Safety signed an MoU on cooperation in health and medicine. The two sides also signed a government-to-government agreement on cooperation in Ayurveda and other traditional systems of medicine.The remaining two agreements provide for technical cooperation in sustainable urban development and collaboration in livestock and fisheries development.Balen Shah highlights shared ties, climate cooperationAt the joint press conference, Balen Shah described India-Nepal relations as being founded on mutual respect, trust and goodwill.“Ties between India and Nepal stand as firm as the Himalayas and as vast as oceans,” he said.He expressed confidence that the agreements and initiatives announced during the visit would take bilateral relations to a new level, while stressing the need for cooperation on climate change.“I am confident that these historic milestones will elevate Nepal-India relations to new heights. The need of the hour is to build on the strong foundation of this enduring relationship and lay solid pillars for the future. Our Himalayas, the sources of clean water, sustain millions across this region. The pristine rivers flowing from the Himalayas into the Ganga remind us of our future and destiny, underscoring the need to address the challenges of climate change through collective action. Nepal and India have been bound by historical, cultural and civilisational ties since the sacred era of Lord Ram and Mata Janaki,” Balen Shah said.Balen Shah's first bilateral visit to IndiaBalen Shah arrived in New Delhi on Sunday for a two-day state visit, his first to India since assuming office in March 2026.On Monday, PM Modi received him at Hyderabad House for the bilateral talks. Before the meeting, Shah was accorded a ceremonial welcome at Rashtrapati Bhavan and paid floral tributes to Mahatma Gandhi at the Raj Ghat memorial.Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in a post on X that the leaders would discuss various aspects of bilateral relations and explore new avenues to deepen cooperation.Jaiswal described the ceremonial welcome as reflecting “the special warmth and enduring friendship between India and Nepal” and Shah’s visit to Raj Ghat as “A tribute to the timeless legacy of Mahatma!”Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: The four finalists who will battle it out for the 28th annual Turnip Prize are announced.
articles.body:
The finalists of an annual spoof art competition have been announced.

The Turnip Prize, held at The New Inn in Wedmore, Somerset, celebrates the most ridiculous or rubbish piece of modern art created with the least amount of effort possible. Those that display "too much effort" are immediately disqualified.

The competition - which began in 1999 - satirises the Tate Gallery's prestigious Turner Prize.

Organisers received 69 entries from around the world this year, but Costa Living, Massive Data Leek, Stockpile and Traffic Jam were selected as the four finalists. The winner will receive a turnip impaled on a rusty nail on 8 December.

The Turnip Prize began in 1999 in response to Tracey Emin's My Bed, which was shortlisted for the Turner Prize that year.

articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg turned his wife Priscilla Chan into a GTA 6 character who asks him to bring groceries, and the meme drew a laughing reply from Elon Musk and jokes that he got the errands version
articles.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has joined the growing wave of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) memes, giving the internet an unexpected glimpse of what his version
articles.body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has joined the growing wave of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) memes, giving the internet an unexpected glimpse of what his version of the game might look like. Zuckerberg shared an edited screenshot featuring his wife, Priscilla Chan, as an in-game character assigning him a grocery-shopping task. Instead of the action-packed missions associated with the popular video game, the notification asked him to pick up groceries and bring them home, adding that Priscilla would appreciate the gesture. Zuckerberg accompanied the image with a playful question about which version of the game he had received. The post quickly attracted attention on X, with Tesla CEO Elon Musk responding with a laughing emoji and users joining in with jokes about the billionaire's virtual household duties.Mark Zuckerberg gives GTA 6 a domestic twist with Priscilla Chan memeZuckerberg shared the meme on X on November 20, 2026, shortly after the release of GTA 6. The edited screenshot featured a mission notification titled "Pick up Groceries", followed by the instruction: "Buy some groceries and bring them back to the house."The notification also carried the message, "Priscilla will appreciate this", replacing the game's female protagonist Lucia with Zuckerberg's wife.Adding to the humour, Zuckerberg captioned the post: "Wait which version did I get?" The joke played on the contrast between the game's reputation for action-packed missions and the rather ordinary household responsibility assigned to him in the edited image.Elon Musk reacts as internet jokes about Zuckerberg's errands versionThe post attracted reactions from social media users, including Elon Musk, who responded with a laughing emoji. His reaction added another high-profile name to the conversation surrounding Zuckerberg's gaming joke.Other users also joined the exchange, with one commenting, "Looks like you got the errands version", alongside an edited image of a game character performing household chores.Another user joked about Zuckerberg joining the trend before the next instalment in the franchise, writing, "Lmao we got Zuck making GTA memes before GTA 7."Some users also questioned whether the Meta chief would ever be the one personally doing the grocery shopping, extending the joke beyond the fictional mission.How GTA 6's grocery-shopping missions became an internet memeThe joke draws on a feature of GTA 6 that has become a popular subject of online discussion. The game includes everyday relationship-related tasks involving Jason and his girlfriend Lucia, including buying groceries, bringing her flowers and fixing up the house.The game's notification prompts suggest that completing these activities will make Lucia appreciate Jason's efforts. One such message, featuring the phrase "Lucia will appreciate this", became the basis for a series of edits across social media.Users began replacing the original character's name and changing the instructions to create humorous versions of the notification. Zuckerberg adapted the format by inserting Priscilla Chan's name into the grocery-shopping prompt, turning an ordinary in-game activity into a joke about married life.The meme has also attracted discussion about the game's portrayal of relationships, with players sharing their reactions to the inclusion of domestic responsibilities alongside the franchise's more familiar action-oriented gameplay.You use AI every day. articles.title: Two dead, three hospitalised after suspected mass drug overdose at California home
articles.summary: Two people died and three others were hospitalised after five people were found suffering from suspected drug overdoses at a home in Northern California
articles.body: Two people died and three others were hospitalised after five people were found suffering from suspected drug overdoses at a home in Northern California on Saturday morning, police said.According to the New York Post, officers from the Oroville Police Department were called to a property in the 100 block of Hammon Park Drive around 8:10 am after receiving reports of multiple people experiencing possible drug overdoses.When officers arrived, they found five people displaying apparent overdose symptoms, including several who had lost consciousness.Police officers immediately began administering emergency medical aid, including performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and using Narcan, a medication that can reverse the effects of an opioid overdose, while waiting for paramedics to arrive.Despite the rescue efforts, two victims died at the scene. articles.title: Occupied West Bank ‘military zones’ become de facto Israeli settler land
articles.summary: Closed military zones in the occupied West Bank are being seized by settlers as staging posts for pogroms.
articles.body:
Ramallah, Occupied West Bank – Saleh Zahran had a room on his family’s land with a television, a fireplace, a fridge and solar panels. The kids would play in the groves, and the men stayed up late at night watching the stars.

“We’d cook, eat, drink, spend a whole day from morning to sunset,” he says.

Zahran, 39, inherited the farmland, with 120 olive trees, in Deir Abu Mishal, a village west of Ramallah, from his grandfather and father, splitting it among his brothers.

Between 70 and 80 percent of people in the village, which falls in Area B, under joint Israeli-Palestinian control, live off the land, and just a few years ago, there were no settlers nearby.

“We’d come and go whenever we wanted, pick our fruit at our own pace, sell, build, and marry off sons from the olives. Now, it’s all gone,” he told Al Jazeera.

Since settlers set up an outpost in Area B about 1km from his land in June, nobody in his family had been able to reach it. Settlers attacked their cars, and his elderly father was pepper-sprayed while trying to reach the farmland, he says.

On November 10, an Israeli High Court decision granted the village two days of army “coordinated” harvesting, something once unthinkable in Area B.

Zahran set out with his brothers to reach their lands for the first time in five months, but about 20 settlers came at them. They threw stones, smashed the family’s truck and his brother’s four-wheeler and slashed the tyres. He saw no soldiers, and police never arrived despite their calls.

The next day, the army and its liaison office were present. But farmers were held up until about 9am, shown a map of permitted areas, and told to leave by 2:30pm. Ghiyath Nasser, their lawyer, says villagers could reach less than a third of the area in question, so Zahran could harvest only about 20 of his 120 trees.

After five months, Zahran finally reached the farm room that day only to find settlers had stolen or smashed his belongings and were drawing water for their sheep from the two wells he had restored. The saplings he had planted last year had died of thirst.

On paper, it is the settlers who are barred from the Zahran family’s property and the land around Deir Abu Mishal. But in practice, it is Palestinian owners like Zahran who are kept out.

Nasser says that after his first legal petition, the army twice demolished the outpost – which was immediately rebuilt both times – then declared the site a closed military zone for Israelis only. That, Nasser argues, means soldiers cannot demand permits or “coordination” from Palestinian owners – their job is to keep settlers out.

“Sometimes they declare an area closed to settlers, but in the application they close it to Palestinians,” said Wail Qut, a lawyer with the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center (JLAC), who is from Madama, south of Nablus.

Kerem Navot and Peace Now’s July report found that, at the end of 2025, farm outposts effectively controlled more than 1 million dunams (247,105.4 acres), about 18 percent of the West Bank — roughly 750,000 dunams (185,329 acres) taken since late 2022.

In Madama, closures came first, and the outposts followed. Qut says its northern land was never declared a closed military zone, but the effect was the same.

About five years ago, the army gated the road from the village to Nablus, citing security concerns, he says. It was the only access to as much as a third of Madama’s land. The Israeli High Court dismissed the villagers’ petition after the army said farmers could reach the land on foot or by animal and apply for permits.

“It’s a de facto closure, though,” said Qut, with farmers still barred from entering.

Then, last April, an outpost of what Qut estimates are now 10 caravans appeared inside the closed area. He said the army suddenly reopened the gate for the settlers to use. Qut and his brother were stopped by a settler in the same area when they tried to pick olives there this year, forcing them to leave under armed threat.

Dror Etkes, founder of Kerem Navot, which tracks settler land takeovers, says such closures without orders are common across the occupied West Bank. “There is no vacuum in the West Bank,” he said. “Once an area is closed to Palestinian access, settlers sooner or later will come and take it over, and this is exactly what happened in Madama.”

But Qut finds the courts complicit too. When JLAC petitioned over the outpost north of Madama in September, the court gave the state until May 2027 to respond, rather than a few days, as Qut expected.

On November 13, a wedding was due to take place in al-Mughayyir, located at the northeastern edge of the Ramallah governorate. “Despite the pain and the suffering, people rejoice,” said Samir Abu Alia, 60, a village council member whose cousin’s son, Hassan Abu Alia, 30, was the groom. But soldiers violently cut the festivities short.

“The moment the patrols came down, they surrounded the hall, 20 army jeeps, and started throwing stun grenades between the men and the women,” recalled Abu Alia. Soldiers took the groom and relatives away from his bride for two hours. Abu Alia and others say the groom was beaten.

It began earlier that day on the eastern plain, when a settler grazing his flock inside a closed military zone claimed someone from al-Mughayyir had thrown firecrackers or shot at him, although he was unhurt. Soldiers accepted the settler’s claim at face value and then sealed and raided the village. The army quickly targeted the wedding, claiming there were gunshots and firecrackers, which attendees deny.

About 80 percent of al-Mughayyir’s 43,000 dunams (10,625.5 acres) lies beyond its eastern entrance, closed for years. Abu Alia says villagers can now move freely in only about 900 dunams (222.4 acres). “The rest of the land they’ve taken over, they stop people from reaching it, on the pretext of a military zone, on the pretext of security, on the pretext of I don’t know what.”

Here, the outpost came first. Village council member Marzouq Abu Naim says the first outpost on the eastern plain appeared in 2018 and has grown from 200 dunams to 5,000 dunams. He counts a dozen around the village. “One of the settlers comes, brings a tent, pitches it on a hilltop … the second day, the third day, you find there’s facilitation, something not normal: [authorities] run him water, they run him electricity, they lay a road to this tent,” he said.

According to Abu Naim, when villagers tried to use the eastern entrance about two months ago, settlers attacked and tried to burn cars and tractors, and the army did nothing to intervene.

Abu Naim, whose son, Jihad, 32, was shot dead by a settler during an invasion of the village school in April, also lost a 10-dunam grove of about 250 olive trees. “It wasn’t me who planted them, or my father — our grandfathers planted them.”

In August 2025, after a shooting wounded an Israeli teenager, the army ordered olive trees beside a settler road through the plain cleared as a “security threat”, and settlers joined in. Locals say more than 10,000 trees were eventually uprooted, including 230 belonging to Abu Alia.

Documents from the Israeli NGO Yesh Din show the area was closed for 30 days to “preserve the aims of the clearing”. Renewed in October 2025, the order extended to July 2026 with redrawn boundaries, and again through December.

The order bars everyone without a permit, settlers included. But Yesh Din’s legal objection says it is enforced only against the owners, while settlers graze, plough and build on their plots. When the army’s legal adviser declined to enforce the closure against settlers, he referred Yesh Din to the Israeli Defence Ministry’s legal adviser instead, which the NGO says was an effort to absolve the army of responsibility.

Lior Zur, a Yesh Din lawyer representing the petitioners, told Al Jazeera, “Through this policy of selective enforcement, the military turns closure orders into a mechanism for transferring possession of land from its lawful Palestinian owners to settler trespassers.”

The pattern runs across the West Bank. In March, a closed zone around Duma was enforced against Israeli solidarity activists protecting Bedouin families, rather than settlers; after soldiers removed the activists, settlers invaded the encampment, forcibly displacing the community the next day.

In Burin , farmland sits in closed zones renewed every month or two; settlers have gutted five greenhouses in these closed zones already. In Taybeh , an August order barred Israelis and foreigners, but settlers and outposts remained, including one near the edge of Area B that led to another unevenly enforced closed zone.

Similar cases have occurred in Ein al-Duyuk , Qusra , Umm al-Khair and elsewhere. In closed and firing zones the Israeli army has not used for decades, Etkes said, settlers are “filling in”, even though the orders formally apply to settlers, too.

The result, this olive harvest season, has been unprecedented levels of violence and access restrictions. The United Nations Humanitarian Country Team for the occupied Palestinian territory said on November 20 that more than 400 settler attacks that caused casualties or damage had been recorded since September, more than in any previous season. The infrequent “coordination” access windows, it said, are often followed by “cancellations, denial of entry, expulsion or attacks”.

“What started as local initiative has been adopted by the military and is today, maybe not a declared policy, but an implemented policy,” said Etkes. The outposts are “not legal, but they are completely supported by the military, by the government, without officialising it”. The Israeli Civil Administration has leased large areas of the West Bank to settlers for grazing, which they never do for Palestinians, Qut said.

“Military closed-zone orders and settler takeovers of Palestinian land are two complementary practices,” said Yair Dvir, spokesperson for Israeli NGO B’Tselem. “The military uses these orders to drive Palestinians off their land, while settlers are frequently allowed to remain or establish outposts.”

Back in Deir Abu Mishal, olives are rotting on trees as the season ends. Zahran’s three young children ask why they cannot return to the farm room for barbecues and the olive harvest. He tells them it is too dangerous. “Four or five settlers stop a whole village, 5,000-6,000 people, from going to the land,” Zahran said. “We are living the height of injustice.”

articles.title: Cardiff woman with appendicitis warns of antibiotic resistance
articles.summary: Harriet Davies was given the drugs after falling ill while skiing in France.
articles.body:
Holidaymaker Harriet Davies was left fighting for her life after suffering side effects from drugs she believed would help her.

The 37-year-old fell ill with appendicitis while skiing in France in January.

After having surgery and being given medication there Davies, from Cardiff, returned home. But the pain persisted.

On returning to hospital, a scan revealed an abscess in her abdomen and she was given antibiotics.

But Davies became sicker. She vomited and had a fever and was given different antibiotics.

Davies said while the drugs worked she was left with sore lips and a rash.

Antibiotic resistance like this happens when bacteria do not respond to medicines designed to treat them, making infections harder to treat.

"I got a fever, and a blood test showed that my immune system had completely crashed," she said.

"The type of white blood cell that protects against infection was basically gone, I didn't have any of that which was the first line of defence.

"So, I had to go back to hospital then and have emergency antibiotics to basically stop me from getting sepsis."

Davies believed the antibiotics made her ill.

She said: "I started realising that it wasn't going the way they had expected and seeing the reaction of the clinical team around me, that was really scary for me.

"I started to realise that this is really serious and my life is potentially at risk here if I don't get better from this infection."

It was weeks before Davies got better. She urged others to be aware of drugs' side effects.

"[Antibiotics] saved my life ultimately but they also made me quite ill and I now see them as something that should only be used when they're really, really needed," she said.

"My experience highlights how quickly bacterial infections can become complicated and potentially dangerous, and how hard they can be to treat when antibiotic options are limited, particularly if someone develops a severe reaction to a treatment."

Davies and Public Health Wales (PHW) now want people to be aware of the dangers of antimicrobial resistance, or resistance to antibiotics.

The matter is being highlighted by World Antimicrobial Resistance Awareness Week, which runs until 24 November.

PHW's consultant antimicrobial pharmacist Dr Nicholas Reid said it was a misunderstanding that antibiotic resistance only affected people who took antibiotics often.

Anyone, he said, could pick up an antibiotics-resistant infection.

"When antibiotics don't work as expected, people may need alternative treatments or longer hospital care," he said.

"Protecting their effectiveness is vital, not just for treating infections but also for procedures such as surgery and cancer care."

Swansea University's Prof Thomas Wilkinson called antibiotic resistance a burden on every hospital in the world.

There were, he said, other "strategies" but he warned: "They cost money."

articles.title: Capita shares plunge 70% as boss quits after civil service pensions failure
articles.summary: Public sector workers have been hit by delays to pension payments, in a scheme overseen by Capita since last year.
articles.body:
Shares in outsourcing business Capita have sunk 70% after its boss stepped down as the saga over public sector pensions drags on.

Chief executive Adolfo Hernandez has agreed with the firm's board to leave with "immediate effect", admitting that the company had "not delivered" for members of the UK's Civil Service pension scheme.

The scheme, which manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK, has been mired in controversy, with tens of thousands of retiring civil servants having faced delays receiving their pension payments.

Capita has cut its profit forecast, partly due to the problems surrounding the scheme, and says it plans to raise £190m to bolster its finances.

Capita took over the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme in December last year.

One Cabinet Office minister last month labelled the company's progress in improving how it runs the scheme as "abysmal".

Hernandez, who will be replaced by current chief financial officer Pablo Andres, said: "I am proud of the groundwork we have laid and the progress we have made under my leadership.

"Of course, within that I recognise that we have not delivered the service that members of the Civil Service pension scheme deserve."

Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules

Capita said it was now expecting its underlying operating profit for 2027 to be hit by between £85m and £95m, having previously expected a reduction of up to £40m.

This comes from the extra cost of the recovery plan, as well the loss of two other "major" contracts in the defence and pension solutions divisions.

Capita said it was planning an equity raise of £190m in the first half of next year, in order for the company to "move forward from a more stable foundation".

The backlog of payments from the civil service pension scheme has been described as "hell" by people who have failed to receive money, some of whom retired early owing to ill health.

BBC Radio 4's Money Box programme has been hearing from people caught up in the saga , and left in financial hardship.

Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the Public Accounts Committee of MPs, said: "The mishandling of the civil service pension scheme has caused severe hardship for some scheme members, particularly considerably delayed bereavement payments.

"The PAC will continue to pursue this dreadful matter and we can only hope that the new acting Chief Executive, Pablo Andres, will be able to get a grip on this whole affair."

Until the end of November 2025, the scheme was administered by a company called MyCSP.

The contract was taken over by Capita on 1 December, in a seven-year deal worth £239m.

"Capita inherited an enormous backlog of cases which needed addressing and failed to deliver on the promised automation, AI and digital tools needed to manage the 1.7 million members," said Russ Mould, investment director at investment platform AJ Bell.

"Efforts to fix the problems failed and government deadlines came and went, leading to the withholding of milestone payments, with the National Audit Office probing the contract.

"Capita needs to steady the ship quickly, and hope that the modest recent improvements in service levels on the civil service scheme can be built upon."

articles.title: Nigeria's Bola Tinubu: Aso Rock suffers water and power cuts
articles.summary: Bola Tinubu says he was shaving last week when the water cut out - an experience familiar to many Nigerians.
articles.body:
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - issues that are all too common for the country's ordinary citizens.

He said he was shaving last week when the water supply cut at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja.

He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues.

Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.

He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [there’s punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].

"The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.

Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.

Can Nigeria's president regain voters' trust after painful first term?

Search and rescue teams race against time after Nigeria boat tragedy

Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.

Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.

The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure, leaving millions without reliable supplies, especially in Lagos.

Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the election on 16 January 2027.

In 2022, months before the last presidential election, Tinubu said: "Whichever way, by all means necessary, you will have electricity, and you will not pay for estimated bills any more. A promise made will be a promise kept.

"If I don't keep the promise and I come for a second term, don't vote for me, unless I give you adequate reasons why I couldn't deliver,” he said.

Despite the continuing power cuts, some of his supporters point to improved electricity supplies in rural areas as well as a recently approved $2bn (£1.5bn) investment in a new East–West Super Grid, designed to expand electricity transmission capacity and strengthen the national grid, as evidence that he is doing his best to keep to his promise.

Tinubu defeated the country’s former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as former Anambra state governor Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

articles.title: Prepare for more tech outages amid ‘urgent’ upgrades, says US intelligence chief
articles.summary: ‘We are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service’ due to decades-old digital infrastructure, says Jay Clayton
articles.body:
People should prepare for more technology outages and disruptions to digital services , according to US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.

In an interview with CNN, Mr Clayton warned that decades-old systems are undergoing urgent upgrades to improve security against emerging cyber threats like autonomous artificial intelligence agents.

"The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cyber security , and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road," Mr Clayton said.

"You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot."

His comments come after a series of major tech failures that caused outages to critical services and digital infrastructure.

These have included a global Microsoft outage – which knocked out emails for governments, doctor surgeries and businesses – as well as a communications failure with the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) that grounded flights for several hours.

Mr Clayton said investment was needed to improve cyber security and protect increasingly sophisticated and exposed networks.

"As part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service," Mr Clayton said. "That ​is ⁠going to happen."

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reiterated the warning on CBS, saying that there could be some issues with updates introduced by banks to protect against AI .

"The patches may cause a glitch," he said. "I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine; your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency."

The White House recently moved to overhaul its cyber security leadership, naming Kirsten Davies as the new National Cyber Director after Sean Cairncross stepped aside.

In her new role she will oversee cyber security policy and strategy across the federal government.

"Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected," she wrote in a post on X.

"Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come… But only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future."

articles.title: COP31: What next after UN climate talks collapse
articles.summary: UN member states fail to agree on how to fast-track action to reverse global warming in a blow to climate agenda.
articles.body:
United Nations climate talks have ended in collapse after countries deadlocked over the phasing out of planet-warming fossil fuels, aiding energy transition for developing countries and the response to natural disasters.

Known as COP31, the conference in Antalya, Turkiye, ended on Sunday as the European Union and others ⁠⁠rejected a final deal they said was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.

The longest UN climate summit on record brought to the fore the divide between major polluters driving climate change and smaller nations bearing the brunt of its impact, after a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Asia .

It also laid bare the world’s inability to keep the Paris Agreement pledge to limit global warming to the 1.5C (2.7F) mark , which scientists expect to overshoot in a few years.

So what’s next for the fraught UN process and what else can nations do to deliver promises that have too often missed their target?

The 11-day-long negotiations that began on November 9 were stalled after oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels in the final deal put forward by the president of COP31, Turkiye, and main negotiator Australia.

Saudi Arabia and fellow members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) opposed any mention of a fossil fuel phase-out, while insisting instead on carbon capture , the technology criticised as costly and ineffective.

Cosima Cassel, programme lead in Climate Diplomacy and Geopolitics at ⁠⁠environmental think tank E3G, said petrostates attempted to slow momentum on the energy transition “following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz and the projected decline in their incomes as global demand for fossil fuels falls”.

The European Union and several nations particularly vulnerable to climate change said they could not accept a text that failed to mention the ⁠⁠main driver of global warming.

The revised text of a deal that emerged early on Sunday was angrily rejected after some 130 nations sent a letter to the presidency stating that a deal would have to mention a path for transitioning away from fossil fuels.

On the contrary, the text made no mention of fossil fuels while promoting carbon capture.

“A small group of blockers set the outcome against the clear position of a large majority,” Cassel told Al Jazeera. “These dynamics raise questions about the role of oil and gas exporters in undermining the only forum where vulnerable countries get to advance their concerns.”

Crucially for developing countries, there was also no progress on the funds needed to help them transition their energy systems and respond to natural disasters.

Under the 2015 Paris Agreement , developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations. However, the US-Israeli war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine strained national budgets, leaving wealthy nations unwilling to commit trillions of dollars in climate finance.

Sebastien Duyck, senior attorney at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL), said wealthy developed countries, which denounced the obstruction by fossil fuel-producing nations, showed “considerable hypocrisy”.

“You cannot demand a just transition from others while failing to pay your fair share of its costs,” Duyck told Al Jazeera. “We need less finger-pointing and political theatre and more accountability. All major economies, particularly the wealthiest, must deliver on their existing legal obligations and climate finance commitments ahead of COP32.”

What’s next for the UN process – and for the planet?

The collapse of the climate talks in Turkiye has renewed questions about reform of its consensus-based process, centred around the principle that all countries must agree to the reforms.

The commitment to moving away from fossil fuels – including natural gas, coal and crude oil – was considered a landmark achievement of COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. But even then, the deal stopped short of calling for a “phase-out”, amid fierce lobbying from oil-producing countries.

Amid concern that fossil fuel producers wield more power than those who want to accelerate the transition to a low-carbon world, many believe the COP process remains important as a platform that brings together virtually every country in the world.

“The UN process remains the only forum where every country has a voice and a chance to shape outcomes and it is worth protecting and fighting for,” said E3G’s Cassel.

However, calls for reform are multiplying and a second tier of COPs – the Global Climate Action Agenda – is rising in prominence. Often called just the Action Agenda, the voluntary implementation pillar of the UN Climate Change process is bringing in real-world actors such as financial institutions, cities, regions, businesses and civil society on a voluntary basis.

“That spirit of collaboration stands in stark contrast to the adversarial dynamics that too often dominate the formal negotiations,” Cassel said.

Other routes are also being pursued. An International Court of Justice advisory opinion last year confirmed that states have a binding legal obligation to combat climate change. In April, the Santa Marta initiative convened 57 countries to promote non-binding cooperation around fossil fuel phase-out.

Duyck, at CIEL, said “the failure of governments to agree at this conference does not make the science any less clear or their legal obligations any less binding.” “A fair and orderly transition away from fossil fuels remains both an imperative and a collective responsibility,” he added.

The UN Environment Programme last year said the world would exceed the 1.5C (2.7F) mark – the internationally agreed-upon target set under the Paris Agreement – “very likely” within the next decade.

Without any meaningful action, the planet will warm 2.3 to 2.5C (4.1 to 4.5F) by 2100, the report said.

Joeri Rogelj, professor of climate science and Policy at Imperial College London, said a starting point would have been to renew commitments made at COP28 in Dubai, where nations had agreed to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems, triple renewable energy capacity globally and double the global average annual rate of energy efficiency improvements by 2030.

Instead, “even simply echoing these agreed outcomes was politically too challenging for some countries with strong vested interests in fossil fuels,” he told Al Jazeera.

“The commitments needed are clear: global greenhouse gas emissions must decline to slow the rate of global warming,” Rogelj told Al Jazeera.

“This failure risks further delaying meaningful global emissions reductions, with the poorest and most vulnerable countries and communities bearing the greatest consequences.”

articles.title: Nigeria boat accident: At least 29 dead after overcrowded boat capsizes in Bayelsa
articles.summary: The government blames overcrowding, poor maintenance, and missing life jackets for boat accidents.
articles.body:
Nigerian search and rescue teams are racing against time to find survivors after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.

Twenty-nine bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued so far, a spokesperson for the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) told the BBC.

The government has responded by ordering stricter enforcement of safety standards on the country's inland waterways.

Overcrowding, poor maintenance and failure to observe safety regulations have contributed to previous deadly accidents on Nigeria's rivers.

The boat was travelling from Ayama community when it developed mechanical problems, according to police spokesperson Musa Mohammed.

Passengers asked the boat operator to steer towards land, but he allegedly declined, leading to the accident.

Survivors have described the panic that followed as passengers struggled to swim and stay afloat while waiting for emergency rescue services.

"As I swam, people were dragging me to the bottom, and I bit one woman and saved myself," Charity Ebikaboaere told local media outlet Arise News.

"Our things, our money, phones, everything lost, but me and my siblings are alive," said another survivor, Tari Samuel.

Why do Nigeria's boat disaster keep happening?

Nema spokesman Manzo Ezekiel raised concerns about the use of untrained boat operators and passengers travelling without life jackets.

"Some of them believe they're from river areas and they know how to swim," he said, warning that familiarity with waterways should not replace basic safety precautions.

There have been reports that the boat was carrying more than 300 people but the Nema spokesperson said this wasn't correct. He did not say how many people were on board but said it was overcrowded.

The accident happened in a region where waterways are a key means of transport, especially for communities with limited road access.

"Overloading, speeding, recklessness and traveling without life jackets must stop. No journey is worth a life," Bayelsa Commissioner for Information Ebiuwou Koku-Obiyai said in a statement on Saturday.

Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has relayed his condolences to the victims' families.

In a statement posted on X, Tinubu said he had directed relevant federal disaster response agencies to work together to ensure a successful rescue and recovery operation.

He also ordered that his election rally on Saturday, in Ibadan, Oyo State, be held without much fanfare in honour of those who lost their lives.

Boat accidents are a recurring problem in Nigeria, particularly in riverine communities where boats are a major means of transport.

In August, at least 50 people, mostly children, died after an overloaded boat capsized in the north-western Sokoto state. In January, at least 25 people died when a leaking boat capsized in Yobe state, in the north-east.

articles.summary: A search for a missing baby in South Carolina ended in a discovery that left rescuers stunned: an 11-month-old boy was found alive beneath freshly
articles.body: A search for a missing baby in South Carolina ended in a discovery that left rescuers stunned: an 11-month-old boy was found alive beneath freshly disturbed earth, trapped inside a dog crate wrapped in a towel. After nearly 24 hours underground, the infant, identified as Koah Sharp, was heard crying as officers dug through the soil in a wooded area. What began as a missing-child emergency had turned into a race against time, with investigators later suggesting that a small pocket of trapped air inside the crate may have helped keep him alive. According to PBS News and CBS News, the child has since been released from hospital and is expected to make a full recovery.Nearly 100 rescuers joined the searchKoah was reported missing on Monday in Lexington County, an area west of Columbia, South Carolina. Authorities said the infant had been staying with his grandmother, Patricia Comer, when she left to run an errand.His father, 25-year-old Michael Comer, was temporarily entrusted with the child's care while another caregiver was expected to arrive. However, when the scheduled caregiver reached the house, both the father and the infant had disappeared.According to PBS News, investigators examined surveillance footage from several local businesses, which showed Comer travelling around the area without the baby. The father was eventually located and arrested on Monday night.Meanwhile, nearly 100 law enforcement officers and public safety personnel participated in the extensive search for the missing infant.Freshly disturbed soil led officers to the babyThe breakthrough came when search teams noticed an unusual patch of freshly disturbed earth in a wooded area approximately 50 yards from the home of Koah's paternal grandfather Sheriff Bryan Koon, PBS News states.As officers began digging, they heard a baby crying beneath the ground. They found a towel-wrapped dog crate with the missing infant after their efforts, the report adds.“We located him and it was a desperate rescue attempt,” Sheriff Bryan Koon told CBS News. “Officers rushed to get him out of the buried enclosure.”PBS News reported that the sheriff said the crate had been buried relatively shallowly, with approximately a foot of soil covering its upper surface.Koah was found covered in dirt and in an extremely vulnerable condition. His cries alerted rescuers to his presence and helped them locate him before it was too late, the report adds.Towel may have created an air pocketOne of the most significant questions investigators faced was how the infant managed to survive underground for approximately 24 hours.According to PBS News, Sheriff Koon suggested that the towel wrapped around the crate may have created an air pocket, allowing the child to breathe despite being buried. Cooler temperatures in the area may also have played a role in helping him survive.CBS News reported that Koah was immediately transported to a hospital following his rescue. He was released on Tuesday night, and medical professionals indicated that he was expected to make a full recovery. The infant is now staying with family members.Father faces multiple criminal chargesMichael Comer was arrested after being found hiding inside an outbuilding in Batesburg-Leesville, according to CBS News. Arrest warrants cited by the broadcaster listed charges of attempted murder, unlawful conduct toward a child, custodial interference and burglary.PBS News initially reported that Comer was being held without bond on a burglary charge while investigators worked with prosecutors to establish additional charges.The sheriff's department also confirmed that the child's parents had a history of domestic violence-related issues. Court records cited by the Associated Press showed that Comer had been sentenced to probation in October after pleading guilty to domestic violence and aggravated breach-of-peace charges stemming from a July arrest. A gun charge was dropped as part of the plea agreement.Investigation continues after miraculous rescueAlthough Koah's survival brought relief to his family and rescuers, authorities continued investigating the circumstances surrounding his disappearance and burial. articles.title: Inside the talks between student protest leaders and Macron’s government
articles.summary: Al Jazeera interviews two French student leaders who have met with top government officials as protests continue.
articles.body:
Paris, France – High school student Marius Mensil has participated in several meetings with top officials, including President Emmanuel Macron, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, and Education Minister Edouard Geffray, aimed at addressing the concerns of thousands of protesting students.

“They’re very good at listening to us. They welcome us, smile at us, tell us, ‘Yes, you’re right, your demands are legitimate’, and in the end, they do nothing,” the 17-year-old told co-leader of the French high-school students’ union, Union Syndicale Lyceenne (USL), told Al Jazeera.

Held in government offices in Paris, the meetings have, on occasion, lasted as long as two hours, he said.

“With Geffray, it was mainly an exchange of arguments. We’d present our demands to him, and then he’d try to explain why they weren’t feasible,” said Mensil. “He used very technical language to try to confuse us. Macron and Lecornu were much more attentive. They took notes, smiled and gave us winks – in short, they did everything they could to show us that our demands were being heard. All of this, of course, was just a way to avoid making any concrete commitments.”

The student movement first began at high schools in the overseas territory of Mayotte. Then it moved to mainland France, with a high school in Creteil, a suburb southeast of Paris in the Val-de-Marne region, on September 17. Protests quickly spread to neighbouring Saint-Denis and the rest of France, and were joined by groups with other grievances.

For two months, students have blocked their schools’ entrances and taken to the streets, demanding an overhaul of the education system.

“It’s been clear ever since Macron took office – and even before – that conditions have deteriorated year after year. With every budget, there are fewer teachers. There are cuts to local governments, who manage school facilities,” Mesnil told Al Jazeera. “We’re not asking for five-star restaurants, MacBooks, or castles… We’re asking for enough teachers, buildings where the ceilings aren’t falling on our heads and class schedules adapted to our biological rhythms.

“We’re asking that, once we’ve earned our high school diploma, we can study at university.”

In response to the protests, officials invited high school students to voice their concerns. Since late October, representatives have attended several meetings, but despite some concessions, students say their demands remain unmet.

A key demand is to entirely reconstruct Parcoursup, the university admissions programme. Students claim the system is discriminatory and lacks transparency, with rejected students saying they are unable to find out why they were not accepted. The system and some degree programmes also value the academic standing of an applicant’s high school, meaning top students in disadvantaged areas may be overlooked.

They are also calling for an emergency plan to renovate failing school infrastructure. Some student groups and unions also want more teachers on permanent contracts and an additional 10 billion euros ($11bn) devoted to education.

In response to the protests, the government recruited 920 substitute teachers in early October and plans to hire 3,000 more. Next year’s budget includes an increase to cover more substitute hours for each high school.

The government also agreed to commit 1 billion euros ($1.1bn) per year through 2030 to building renovations, and to offer more opportunities for high school representatives to participate in national education discussions.

When contacted by Al Jazeera, the Ministry of Education responded with a statement that Geffray and the minister of higher education, research and space, Philippe Baptiste, sent to students on October 26.

In that statement, the education minister promised to cap class sizes at 28 students at the start of the next academic year in 2027 at “the most disadvantaged schools”, and reduce specialised course sizes. Although some high school students are still calling for Parcoursup to be abolished, the government has agreed to update the controversial platform “to help you plan your academic path with greater peace of mind”.

“Some measures will be implemented very quickly, while others will be included in the 2027 budget bill, which will be introduced in the coming weeks,” Geffray said.

Mesnil called the measures “a few crumbs”, but believes the concessions show that the student movement is making waves.

“The government is starting to give in,” he said. “Gen Z, together with the workers, have forced Macron to back down on some initial points, and we’re very happy about that.”

Beyond meetings, the government opened “High school students, the floor is yours”, a consultation platform for students to submit their opinions and complaints. More than 100,000 submissions were sent in during the 18 days it was open, starting on October 6. About 70 percent said the current school system is “ill-suited to their needs”, citing days that are too long and intense, with poorly structured schedules.

Many French high school students are in class from 8am to 6pm, with few breaks and heavy homework on top of the course load.

More than half of respondents, 56.3 percent, said buildings were dilapidated, improperly insulated and poorly equipped. Participating students also cited absent teachers, class sizes, the Parscoursup platform and negative mental health effects.

Students in disadvantaged areas say conditions are even worse in their suburbs.

Bilal Narjissi, 17, from the Paul-Eluard school in Saint-Denis and a member of the Renouveau Lyceen student union, took part in recent meetings with government officials and said they do not include many students from less advantaged schools.

“In schools in the suburbs and in rural areas, roofs have collapsed, there are water leaks, rats, and classes with 30 students,” he said. “Young people today are pushed to pursue higher education, but they aren’t given the means to succeed.”

Narjissi has invited a special adviser to the prime minister to visit Paul Eluard.

“It would be truly symbolic if he were to come by and we could take him on a tour of the high school, show him the conditions there, and talk to him,” Narjissi said.

Narjissi described the first meeting with officials he attended as “very relaxed”, saying they seemed “very open to dialogue”.

But he added that the economy, education and labour ministries “were quite firm in their positions – for example, on reforming the baccalaureate,” Narjissi said, referring to the final high school exam.

The 2018 high school reforms by former Education Minister Jean-Michel Blanquer introduced “more subject concentrations, shortened the final exam, and placed greater emphasis on grades”, according to Rafaela Uzan, research associate for Europe studies at the Council on Foreign Relations. “But critics argue the abundance of concentration options exacerbated social stratification and made school days longer,” she wrote in a recent paper.

Narjissi said the exchange with officials “was still fairly constructive”, but he is unsure if the students are really being heard “because, so far, there still aren’t any real, concrete responses to our expectations”.

Until they receive those, students say they will continue to protest.

“We’ve managed to establish a balance of power through our mobilisation,” he said.

Student representatives were scheduled to meet with the prime minister again on Monday.

“We hope there will be announcements that live up to our expectations. We’re happy to attend these meetings, but if it’s just to talk and, ultimately, there are no concrete political results, then there’s no point,” Mesnil said.

articles.title: Russell Brand's wife says she will 'honor' rules after sharing his prison message on YouTube
articles.summary: The disgraced comedian and actor asked supporters to help his family after he was sentenced to more than 10 years for rape and sexual assault.
articles.body:
Russell Brand's wife, Laura Brand, has said she will "honor" U.K. prison rules after controversially sharing a message from the convicted rapist claiming his innocence.

Former comedian and actor Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Nov. 9 after being found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three more between 2004 and 2009.

In a YouTube video posted on Nov. 15, Laura Brand read a statement from her husband in which he maintained his innocence and urged supporters to help his "treasured wife and family."

The U.K.'s Ministry of Justice (MOJ) last week confirmed it was investigating whether Brand broke prison rules on making public statements. It also asked Google to remove the video because it was "distressing for victims."

Speaking on the couple's YouTube podcast, Sunday Service with the Brands, Laura Brand said on Sunday, "Last week's episode drew a considerable amount of attention, and now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honor that."

She said she would continue to create the couple's Sunday Service podcast, which is posted on Russell Brand's YouTube channel to its 6.6 million subscribers.

Last week, Google reportedly refused a request by the British government to remove the YouTube video featuring Russell Brand's statement, read by his wife.

The Guardian reported that Google had rejected calls to delete the video, which was still live as of Nov. 23.

A Google spokesperson previously told the outlet, "We're aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand's channel from the YouTube partner program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetize on YouTube since then."

An MOJ spokesperson told Yahoo News, "It is only right that the Government asks for content that is distressing for victims to be taken down, and we strongly believe YouTube should remove this content. Removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms."

In response to the video, a woman who accused Brand of raping her when she was 16 condemned it, calling it an "insult" to his victims and questioning why YouTube had allowed the video to be shared.

Mia Latter told the U.K.'s The Jeremy Vine Show , "I was shocked that YouTube put it out, because I feel like they have some kind of responsibility not to let these things be broadcast.

"And it was an insult to all the women that stood trial, and it was an insult to the jurors that gave their time. It's an insult to the criminal justice system."

British news outlets subsequently reported that Brand risked losing prison privileges and having his calls restricted if an investigation finds his message broke the rules.

An official spokesperson for the U.K. prime minister, Andy Burnham, said last week that Brand's statement was "clearly appalling," adding that Burnham expects "action to be taken if he's found to have broken the rules."

Before he was sentenced, Brand posted weekly episodes of Sunday Service with the Brands , a podcast he hosted with his wife.

In the clip, Laura Brand reads out a statement from her husband in which he references God and thanks those who have supported him.

He goes on to say that he is innocent of the crimes for which he has been found guilty.

Brand also said in the statement that he had been moved to HMP Littlehey, a lower-security prison in Cambridgeshire, England. He was previously held at HMP Wandsworth, a high-security facility in London, before being transferred, according to the BBC .

HMP Littlehey is a "Category C" prison in the U.K., meaning prisoners are considered unlikely to attempt escape but are not deemed suitable for an "open prison," the lowest-security category. Inmates are also provided with training and opportunities to develop their own skills to help them resettle in the community upon release.

Brand is expected to serve two-thirds of his prison sentence before being eligible for release.

Latter was one of the women who featured in a 2023 joint investigation into Brand conducted by U.K. newspapers the Sunday Times and the Times and the TV broadcaster Channel 4. She was known under the pseudonym "Alice" but has recently waived her right to anonymity. She did not feature in the recent trial against Brand, who previously denied all allegations contained in the 2023 report.

Since the verdict, six more women have accused Brand of sexual misconduct , according to a separate investigation by the Times and Sunday Times newspapers in London. The claims made by the women, who all spoke under pseudonyms, span the period from 2005 to 2015.

Delivering the sentence earlier this month at Southwark Crown Court, a criminal court in London, judge Joel Bennathan said Brand had acted with a "casual and arrogant disregard."

He said: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say 'no' and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent."

Yahoo News has reached out to Google for comment.
